chapter_theme: Standing in the middle (நடுவு நிலைமை): those who stand in the middle gain knowledge, escape hell and become gods, jnanis and even the Lord, and the poet stands with them; the last verse defines them as those who cling to the Lord's feet and name.
structure_note: Three refrain verses on நடுவுநின்றார் (320 to 322), each ending with the poet or the Lord, then a verse (323) saying who they are.

320.reading: There is no knowledge except for those who stand in the middle; for those who stand in the middle there is no hell; they become good gods, and I too stood in their way.
320.nuance: நடுவு is the Kural's word for fairness, keeping to no side. In Tirumular it is also traditionally taken as the yogic middle, the poise between the two breaths or the central channel; the verse itself does not decide, and both senses stand.

321.reading: The good cloud-coloured one stood in the middle; the good reciter of the four Vedas stood in the middle; some who stood in the middle became jnanis; those who stood in the middle became even the good Lord.
321.nuance: The cloud-coloured one is Vishnu and the reciter of the four Vedas Brahma. நம்பன், the Lord, is a name of Siva; the last line may mean those in the middle become one with him or that the Lord himself stands in the middle.

322.reading: Some who stood in the middle became jnanis, some gods, some the Lord, and I too stood with those who stood in the middle.
322.nuance: A near repetition of 320 and 321. The gradation (jnanis, gods, the Lord) suggests different ends for those who keep the same middle.

323.reading: He alone dissolves all that has come to be; those who stand always holding the Lord's two feet and cling to the holy name of the First are the ones who stand in the middle.
323.nuance: The verse defines the middle by devotion, not by fairness. மூன்றுநின்றார் is obscure: perhaps standing in the three (thought, word, deed) or at the three times of day. நான்று, hanging, suggests clinging to the name.

links.note: The Kural says the world won't count as ruin the low estate of one who stays fair; Tirumular promises those who stand in the middle knowledge, no hell and godhood. The same virtue, given rewards beyond this world.

321 and 322 are near repeats: both say some who stood in the middle became jnanis (நடுவுநின்றார் சிலர் ஞானிகள் ஆவார்) and became the Lord (நம்பனும் ஆமே / நம்பனு மாவார்). 321 begins with the cloud-coloured one and the Veda-reciter standing in the middle; 322 ends with the poet standing among them.

322 ends 'and I too stood with those who stood in the middle' (நடுவுநின்றாரொடு நானும்நின்றேனே), almost the last line of 320 (நடுவுநின்றார்வழி நானும்நின்றேனே). Both list what standing in the middle yields (knowledge, godhood, freedom from hell) and close on the poet's own stand: a near repeat.

Kural 118 makes fairness the balance that first levels itself and leans to no side (சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் ... ஒருபால் கோடாமை). 323 says those who stand in the middle (நடுவாகிநின்றார்) are those who always hold the Lord's two feet and cling to his name. The same word for steadiness is used for leaning to no side in the Kural and for being fixed on one support in Tirumular.
